header:
Date: 2026-08-23
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Novak (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Peregrine Head of Data Science), Miguel Santos (Peregrine Platform Eng), Priya Desai (Peregrine CISO)
summary: Introductory security-and-hosting discovery. Peregrine is evaluating options (hosted, dedicated, private) for inference for logistics optimization models. Top concerns: SOC2/ISO compliance, SSO/SAML + SCIM, RBAC, KMS integration (bring-your-own-key), audit logs & retention, data residency, and cost vs latency tradeoffs. Redwood AE/SE outlined hosting modes, KMS options, audit log granularity, and suggested a pilot comparing hosted vs dedicated. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share compliance artefacts and cost/latency estimates; Peregrine to share infra details and retention policy.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, our SEs Ravi and Elena are with me, and I think we have Peregrine folks — Laura, Miguel, Priya — thanks for your time.
[00:12] Laura Kim: Yeah thanks, appreciate it. Quick note, we only have about 50 minutes so probably want to focus on security/gating and hosting options.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Sounds good. High level, are you evaluating hosted Redwood API first or are you already leaning to dedicated/private?
[00:28] Miguel Santos: We're exploring all three. Our primary asks are compliance-first — SOC2 and ISO, needs to map to our audit, plus SSO integration, and we have some data residency constraints for EU shipments.
[00:40] Priya Desai: Right, and on the key management side we need BYOK and auditability — can't have plain-text logs leaving the VPC.
[00:49] Ravi Patel: Understood. Quick clarity question — is the idea to run inference on sensitive PII-like shipping manifests, or is it more de-identified telemetry?
[00:58] Laura Kim: It's a mix. Most of our model inputs are operational telemetry but there are cases with customer PII. For those we would prefer a private deployment, but we want to understand cost/operational lift.
[01:10] Elena Novak: Ok. On SOC2/ISO, Redwood has SOC2 Type II and we've got an ISO 27001 alignment document — Maya will share redacted reports. For private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM; for hosted we offer BYOK via KMS federation in some regions.
[01:27] Priya Desai: Can you explain the BYOK for hosted — is that a literal key import or do you do envelope encryption where we hold the root?
[01:36] Maya Chen: Good question. For hosted we support envelope encryption — your master key stays in your KMS, we receive short-lived wrapping keys. We also have an option to rotate unwrap keys per deployment. For Dedicated and Private those can be configured to use your KMS endpoints directly inside your VPC.
[01:52] Miguel Santos: So for Dedicated you'd run within Redwood-managed GPUs but with our VPC peering, right? How does network egress work?
[02:02] Ravi Patel: Dedicated is isolated GPU pools assigned to your account, we can put it in your cloud account via a private VPC peering or use a Redwood-managed VPC with strict network ACLs. Egress can be locked down so model data doesn't leave the private subnet unless you opt-in — logs are delivered to your logging endpoint.
[02:19] Priya Desai: Audit logs — how granular are they? We need per-request metadata, user identity, model version, and truncated inputs for repro but no full PII in the logs.
[02:30] Elena Novak: Our audit logs include request id, caller identity (token/service), model id and version, latency, and a payload hash. We can configure redaction rules for inputs and omit raw prompt data from logs. We also support pushing logs to your SIEM (CloudWatch, Splunk, or a syslog).
[02:46] Laura Kim: That sounds promising. What about SAML and SCIM for provisioning? We use Okta and want JIT provisioning and role sync.
[02:56] Maya Chen: We integrate with SAML SSO for console access and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC supports role templates and you can map groups to roles. API keys can be scoped to routes/models.
[03:08] Priya Desai: Who has access to the KV cache or any persisted artifacts?
[03:13] Ravi Patel: By default, the KV cache is ephemeral and tied to model sessions; no persistent KV store is exposed. For Dedicated/Private we can provide guarantees that caches are local to the serving nodes and never persisted to external storage.
[03:25] Miguel Santos: Latency is a factor — hosted is cheaper to get started but we worry about tail latency for our near-real-time scheduling. Any quantized profiles or batching options we should know?
[03:36] Elena Novak: We have continuous batching tunables and latency SLOs per route. For high-priority routes you can pin to a low-latency pool or use the dedicated GPU pool with smaller batch windows. Quantization and kernel selection are part of the model onboarding; we can profile your workload to recommend settings.
[03:52] Laura Kim: Ok — trial question: could we run a small AB test where sensitive traffic goes to Private/Dedicated and non-sensitive to Hosted, with automatic fallback?
[04:00] Maya Chen: Yes, smart routing policy supports that: route by tag (sensitive=true) to private, else to hosted, with fallback if capacity is hit. We can demo that in the pilot.
[04:09] Priya Desai: Data residency: we need EU data to never leave eu-west-1. Does hosting in region guarantee that?
[04:15] Ravi Patel: We have region-aware routing. For hosted, you can pin region. For Dedicated and Private, you deploy into the customer's chosen region — logs and artifacts remain in-region unless you configure cross-region replication.
[04:28] Miguel Santos: How about retention windows? Our compliance team demands 90 days of audit log retention in immutable storage and 180 days for billing records.
[04:37] Elena Novak: We provide configurable retention for logs; default is 30 days in our hosted plan, but enterprise plans can increase retention and set write-once storage or forward to your own S3 with lifecycle rules.
[04:48] Priya Desai: Encryption in transit and at rest — what's the certificate governance?
[04:53] Maya Chen: TLS 1.2+ in transit, mutual TLS for certain private peering options. At rest, AES-256 with KMS-managed keys; for BYOK the master key never leaves your KMS.
[05:03] Laura Kim: Any third-party pen test or vulnerability disclosures?
[05:07] Ravi Patel: We run quarterly pen tests and will share a redacted summary. SOC2 Type II covers a lot of the controls you care about.
[05:15] Miguel Santos: On the identity side, do API tokens support expiry and rotation via SCIM?
[05:21] Elena Novak: Tokens support TTLs and you can configure rotation policies; SCIM handles user provisioning and group membership for role changes.
[05:27] Laura Kim: For the pilot, what are reasonable success criteria? Latency below 120ms p50 for scheduling inference, no data leakage events, integration with Okta, and KMS BYOK working end-to-end.
[05:39] Maya Chen: That sounds workable. We'll propose a pilot plan that measures p50/p95 latency, request throughput, and validate RBAC/SSO/KMS flows.
[05:48] Priya Desai: Cost question: What are the known tradeoffs between hosted vs dedicated re: unit cost and reserved commit?
[05:54] Ravi Patel: Hosted has the lowest friction and pay-as-you-go pricing but higher per-token cost at scale. Dedicated has lower unit cost for committed throughput, predictable latency, and stronger isolation. Private on-prem gives you the most control but requires more ops lift. We'll put together a back-of-the-envelope for your expected qps and model size.
[06:11] Miguel Santos: Can you do an on-prem container for air-gapped? We have one business line in regulated shipping that may need that later.
[06:17] Maya Chen: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped deployments; that usually goes through our enterprise channel with a support contract.
[06:24] Laura Kim: Any gotchas around model updates and version pinning? We want to pin a model for a while during critical flows and only update after QA.
[06:31] Elena Novak: You can pin model versions per route, do canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to a pinned stable version. We keep artifact immutability so you can repro outputs easily.
[06:42] Priya Desai: About the logs again — can we request an architecture where raw prompts never hit Redwood's durable storage and only ephemeral compute sees them?
[06:51] Ravi Patel: Yes — for privacy-sensitive workloads we can guarantee that raw prompt data is only in-memory on serving nodes and is never written to durable storage in hosted or dedicated modes; for private deployments you control that behavior fully.
[07:05] Laura Kim: Great. On compliance docs — how soon can you share SOC2/ISO papers and the KMS integration guide?
[07:11] Maya Chen: I'll share a SOC2 summary and the KMS/federation guide by Wednesday, 2026-08-26.
[07:17] Miguel Santos: We'll share our infra diagram and expected qps by Friday.
[07:20] Priya Desai: We'll need a short security architecture review with your SEs before we greenlight a pilot.
[07:27] Elena Novak: Happy to do a 60-minute technical deep dive focused on KMS, network topology, and log flows.
[07:34] Laura Kim: Timeline — we want to decide within 4 weeks and if pilot looks good, move to a Q4 dedicated commit.
[07:41] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll aim to get docs and the cost estimate in the next week.
[07:45] Miguel Santos: A couple quick clarifications — how are model artifacts stored when you do caching?
[07:50] Ravi Patel: Model artifacts are stored in encrypted object storage in our infra; for dedicated/private we can configure to use your storage or mount them inside your VPC. Cache keys are ephemeral; artifacts are immutable and signed.
[08:02] Laura Kim: Ok thanks. Anything else on the security checklist?
[08:06] Priya Desai: Just audit trail demonstration — I'd like to see a sample event schema.
[08:11] Maya Chen: We'll attach a sample event schema to the SOC2 pack.
[08:15] Laura Kim: Cool. Let's recap next steps — Maya to send docs, Ravi cost estimate, Miguel infra diagram, Priya to share policy. Then schedule the SE deep dive.
[08:26] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone for the time.
[08:30] (call ends)
